clue.text: Trick answer here

definitions.meaning: to deceive or fool someone, to pull a fast one on them
this very entry is the first across clue in the grid, so its answer sits in the one-across slot

explanation.definitionFit: To fool someone is a colloquial idiom with the same words, and the entry is also literally numbered one across.

clue.text: What roughly gets covered by foot

definitions.text: What roughly gets covered by foot

indicators.note: the shuffled word sits inside, covered on both sides by the other piece

parts.note: to foot the bill is to pay it

indicators.note: roughly signals that the letters of the preceding word are rearranged loosely

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what ground a walker covers on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' turns WHAT into ATHW, and 'gets covered by' puts it inside PAY; the whole clue also describes a track walked on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A track or footway is ground that walkers cover on foot.

clue.text: Engineer overturned hire car

indicators.note: overturned means the word for hire is turned upside down, which in a down clue reads backwards

parts.note: to let a property is to hire it out
a Ford is a make of car

explanation.surface: A mechanic flips over a rental vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' turns LET into TEL. Thomas Telford was a Scottish civil engineer famous for bridges and canals.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford was a celebrated Scottish civil engineer, builder of roads, bridges and canals.

clue.text: What may be put on a kipper by t'university people

definitions.text: What may be put on a kipper by t'university people

parts.words: What may be put on a kipper by t'university people
parts.note: a kipper is slang for a sleeper, and university people are the gown as opposed to town, so this is a sleeper's garment for the night

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire-accented question about what academics put on a smoked herring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kipper' looks like the smoked fish but is someone having a kip (a sleep); 'town and gown' sets locals against members of a university.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment worn in bed at night, the sort of robe a sleeper puts on.

clue.text: Cons headless insects

indicators.note: headless means the opening letter is chopped off the word for insects

parts.note: mantis, the praying insect, can be used as its own plural

explanation.surface: Swindles involving decapitated bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cons' looks like swindles but is the noun for opponents, as in pros and cons.
explanation.definitionFit: Cons are those against something, opponents of a proposal.

clue.text: Better prepared lecturer covers one

indicators.note: covers means the word for lecturer goes round the other piece

parts.note: a reader is a senior university lecturer in Britain
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A teacher who is more ready covers one class.
explanation.walkthrough: A READER is a British university rank just below professor.
explanation.definitionFit: More ready, in a state of fuller readiness.

clue.text: Carpets woven in ranges of colour

indicators.note: woven suggests threads interlaced, so the letters of carpets are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rugs made in a variety of hues.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the band of colours produced when light is split by a prism.

clue.text: Station train can pass? Not usually

indicators.note: not usually suggests the words are put in an unusual order, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asks whether a railway terminus is somewhere trains can go through, which is rarely the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not usually' shuffles TRAIN CAN PASS. This is the London terminus, where trains end rather than pass through.
explanation.definitionFit: A major London railway terminus, home of the Eurostar.

clue.text: A number, inverse of function listed in tables primarily

definitions.text: A number, inverse of function listed in tables primarily

parts.words: A number, inverse of function listed in tables primarily
parts.note: the number whose logarithm is a given value, undoing the log function, and once looked up chiefly in printed tables

explanation.surface: A mathematical description of a figure found by reversing a function in reference tables.
explanation.definitionFit: The number obtained by raising the base to a given power, reversing a logarithm, formerly read from printed tables.

clue.text: What could reveal fate with drink consumed?

definitions.text: What could reveal fate with drink consumed?

indicators.note: consumed means the drink is swallowed inside the rearranged letters
could reveal hints that the letters of fate may be rearranged to show something else

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: Asks what tells fortunes once the cup is drained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could reveal' turns FATE into TEAF, and 'consumed' puts ALE inside it; the whole clue describes reading leaves at the bottom of a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune-tellers read the leaves left in a drained cup to foretell the future.

clue.text: Unionist found in patriotic newspapers

indicators.note: found in means the abbreviation goes inside the phrase for patriotic

parts.note: serving the nation, acting for the state

explanation.surface: A loyalist politician appears in nationalist papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' puts U inside FOR THE STATE.
explanation.definitionFit: The press as a whole, regarded as an estate of the realm alongside lords, clergy and commons.

clue.text: He urged cricketers to play up, bowl craftily in practice

definitions.text: He urged cricketers to play up

indicators.note: in means the shuffled letters sit inside the word for practice

parts.note: nets are cricket practice sessions; a net is one such session

indicators.note: craftily suggests cunning manipulation, so the letters of bowl are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricket coach tells players to bowl cleverly during nets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craftily' turns BOWL into WBOL, and 'in' puts it inside NET. Sir Henry Newbolt wrote 'Vitaï Lampada' with its cricketing refrain 'Play up! play up! and play the game!'
explanation.definitionFit: The poet Sir Henry Newbolt wrote the line exhorting schoolboy cricketers to play up and play the game.

clue.text: It involves kneading tissue with hand no end

definitions.text: It involves kneading tissue with hand no end

indicators.note: kneading suggests working dough about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of end are taken out of the pool, signalled by no

explanation.surface: Describes a massage that works the body's tissue with the hands endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TISSUE and HAND together, remove the letters of END ('no end'), and 'kneading' rearranges the rest; the whole clue describes the Japanese pressure massage.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese massage therapy in which the practitioner presses and works the body with fingers and palms.

clue.text: Was member of team left out, allowed to run out

indicators.note: out means the abbreviation is dropped from the word for being in a team

parts.note: to have played for a side

explanation.surface: A dropped player was allowed to leave the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Payed out' is the nautical spelling for letting a rope run out.
explanation.definitionFit: Of a rope or cable, let out gradually; the nautical past tense of pay.

clue.text: Outside broadcast man following ritual

parts.note: OB is the broadcasting abbreviation for outside broadcast
a manservant, someone's man

explanation.surface: A television crew member attends a religious ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: Careful to keep religious rules and customs, devout in practice.

clue.text: Way-out dance coming after Twist

indicators.note: coming after means the dance word is placed behind the twist word

parts.note: to screw something is to twist it
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: An outlandish dance that follows the Twist, the 1960s craze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' looks like the dance craze but means screw.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric or crazy; an oddball person is way-out.

clue.text: Muses about headless snake, right? An easy problem

indicators.note: about means the word for Muses goes round the beheaded snake

parts.note: there were nine Muses in Greek myth

indicators.note: headless means the opening letter of the snake word is dropped

parts.note: a cobra is a venomous snake

explanation.surface: Someone ponders a beheaded serpent and decides the answer is obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'headless' turns COBRA into OBRA, which 'about' puts inside NINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something requiring no thought at all, a decision so obvious it is simple.

clue.text: A lot of shots counter aggression

parts.note: a bar is a counter where drinks are served
rage is violent anger

explanation.surface: Many drinks served at a bar fuel violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shots' look like drinks, which 'counter' encourages, but they are gunfire.
explanation.definitionFit: A concentrated bombardment of artillery fire.

clue.text: Referee, a right nipper

parts.note: something that nips is a biter

explanation.surface: An official is accused of being a proper little biter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nipper' looks like a child but is one who nips.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge who settles a dispute, an umpire.

clue.text: One tree or another around Pennsylvania in retreat

indicators.note: in retreat means the combined piece goes backwards
around means the other tree surrounds the state abbreviation

parts.note: the elm is another tree
PA is the US postal abbreviation for Pennsylvania

explanation.surface: Trees around Pennsylvania falling back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts PA inside ELM to make ELPAM, which 'in retreat' reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree of the genus Acer, whose leaf is on Canada's flag.

clue.text: Red Cross is in shopping mall

indicators.note: in means the pieces sit inside the word for a shopping mall

parts.note: a mart is a market or trading centre
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: A Red Cross volunteer is collecting in a mall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Cross' looks like the charity; Red is the definition, a communist.
explanation.definitionFit: A communist, a follower of Karl Marx; a Red in political slang.

clue.text: In which public discuss some monograph on Einstein

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Members of the public debate part of a book about Einstein.
explanation.definitionFit: A radio or TV programme where listeners call in to air their views.

clue.text: Fare that could get numismatist excited

definitions.meaning: a coin collector would be thrilled by an uncommon coin, a scarce piece of money

explanation.definitionFit: Welsh cheese on toast is a dish, and read as two words it is an uncommon coin, prized by coin collectors.

clue.text: Not, evidently, a fast rider

parts.note: in a down clue, writing ton upwards gives the clue word not

explanation.surface: Says someone is clearly not a speedy motorcyclist.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the wordplay TON UP, read as an instruction in a down entry, makes NOT. A ton-up boy rode a motorbike at 100 mph.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorcyclist who rides at a hundred miles an hour, a speed merchant.

clue.text: Make calculation come right

definitions.meaning: to compute or figure out a sum
to turn out well, succeed in the end

explanation.definitionFit: To figure out a sum, and to end up successfully, are both senses of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Hardy: one normally expected to have Laurel around

indicators.note: around means the comedian's first name goes round the golfing term

parts.note: Stan Laurel was the thin half of the comedy duo Laurel and Hardy
par is the normal or expected standard

explanation.surface: Oliver Hardy, the comic who always had Stan Laurel beside him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like Laurel's partner but means tough and frugal.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere and tough, like the ancient soldiers of Sparta.

clue.text: Worker consumes fruit for nourishment

indicators.note: consumes means the insect word swallows the fruit word

parts.note: an ant is the classic crossword worker
a lime is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A labourer eats fruit to keep going.
explanation.definitionFit: Food, sustenance that feeds the body.

clue.text: Senior churchman wants more Latin with opt out

indicators.note: out signals the letters are thrown out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A bishop demands more Latin in the liturgy, with an option to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: An archbishop with authority over the bishops of a province.
